title: Local phase-space Berry curvature and Hall transport in textured twisted bilayer graphene
abstract: Slow twist-angle and heterostrain textures in twisted bilayer graphene provide a natural route to phase-space Berry geometry. We show that a purely geometric tetrad/shift sector does not generate mixed Berry curvature once the spin connection is treated consistently. By contrast, a projected textured mini-Dirac cone in twisted bilayer graphene acquires genuine mixed phase-space curvature. We analyze a controlled local Hall-bar limit with a one-dimensional texture and mirror $M_x$. In that limit the pseudogauge gradient renormalizes only the longitudinal conductivity along the textured direction, while a dc nonlinear Hall response appears only when an additional valley-odd tilt generates a Berry-curvature dipole. Both geometric responses peak at the same local filling, $μ_{\rm loc}=\sqrt{2}\,m$, providing a gate-tunable fingerprint of their common origin. All local-cone parameters and their texture susceptibilities are extracted from a heterostrained Bistritzer-MacDonald model at $θ=1.3^\circ$. The tilt invoked in the transport estimates corresponds to heterostrain of only $0.03\%-0.2\%$, below values routinely imaged in devices. The resulting theory provides a local analytic framework for textured moiré Dirac materials and cleanly separates geometric, texture-induced, and transport-level ingredients relevant to realistic TBG.
summary: This theoretical work investigates how local texture variations in twisted bilayer graphene generate measurable Berry curvature and Hall transport effects. It rigorously separates the contributions, showing that while geometry alone is insufficient, the coupling to physical strain and tilt generates distinct, measurable signatures in both linear and nonlinear transport coefficients.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the local phase-space Berry curvature and associated Hall transport phenomena in textured twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), aiming to separate geometric contributions from those induced by physical texture variations.
main_result: Genuine mixed phase-space curvature arises only from the projected texture dependence of the local mini-Dirac cone, and a nonlinear Hall response requires a valley-odd tilt generating a Berry-curvature dipole.
method: The analysis employs a controlled local Hall-bar limit, decomposing the current density into Drude, mixed-curvature, and nonlinear Hall components, and utilizing a local analytic framework derived from the Bistritzer-MacDonald model.
model_or_system: The system is textured twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), modeled using a covariant Dirac Hamiltonian near isolated mini-Dirac points. The local physics is described by a projected two-band Hamiltonian parameterized by local texture fields like twist angle and heterostrain.
key_observables: Mixed Berry Curvature ($\Omega_{r i p j}$), longitudinal conductivity ($\sigma_{xx}$), transverse conductivity ($\sigma_{yy}$), and the nonlinear Hall coefficient ($\chi_{yxx}$).
important_parameters: Local filling ($\mu_{	ext{loc}}$), texture fields ($\delta	heta$, heterostrain), and the local cone parameters ($\epsilon_0, \mathbf{w}, m$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to a controlled local Hall-bar patch with mirror symmetry, and the theory provides a local analytic framework.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the controlled local Hall-bar patch setup and show the dependence of the nonlinear Hall signal ($\chi_{yxx}$) on the valley-odd tilt ($w_x$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by separating geometric and projected texture contributions to the Berry curvature. It then analyzes the linear response ($\sigma_{yy}$ correction) and finally derives the nonlinear Hall response ($\chi_{yxx}$) by focusing on the Berry-curvature dipole term.
why_interesting: The clean separation of geometric vs. texture-induced Berry curvature effects provides a powerful, testable theoretical tool for understanding topological transport in moiré materials, which is relevant to engineered quantum states.
